clinicalPearls: AFib is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the fibrinogen A alpha-chain gene (FGA), producing a variant circulating fibrinogen that is amyloidogenic.
It is among the commonest forms of hereditary systemic amyloidosis in several Western populations and a leading hereditary cause of renal amyloid.
The phenotype is overwhelmingly renal, with hypertension, heavy proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome and relatively rapid progression to end-stage kidney disease.
Glomeruli are characteristically almost completely replaced by amyloid, often with sparing of vessels and interstitium, which is a helpful histological clue.
Penetrance is variable and a family history may be absent, so genetic testing is warranted even in apparently sporadic renal amyloid.
The variant fibrinogen is synthesised by the liver, so combined liver and kidney transplantation can be curative by removing the protein source and replacing the failed organ.
Amyloid may recur in a kidney-only allograft because the amyloidogenic protein continues to be produced.
reference.pathophysiology: Point mutations or frameshift changes in the C-terminal region of the fibrinogen A alpha-chain produce a variant protein that circulates alongside normal fibrinogen. The variant is prone to misfold and deposit as amyloid fibrils, with a striking predilection for the renal glomerulus, where progressive accumulation obliterates the glomerular tuft and drives proteinuria and renal failure. Because the abnormal chain is synthesised by the liver, the amyloid load is sustained by ongoing hepatic production, and extrarenal deposition is usually mild, distinguishing AFib from other hereditary amyloidoses. The rate of progression varies between kindreds and with the specific mutation.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary amyloidoses (lysozyme, apolipoprotein A-I, LECT2)
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with Congo red staining showing glomerular-predominant amyloid
Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry and immunohistochemistry
Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis
SAP scintigraphy to assess organ burden
redFlags: Nephrotic syndrome with rapidly declining renal function
Family history of renal failure or amyloidosis
reference.prognosis: Renal survival is limited once nephrotic syndrome develops, but the systemic course is often more indolent than AL amyloidosis. Combined liver and kidney transplantation can be curative, whereas isolated renal transplantation risks graft amyloid recurrence.
pitfalls: Labelling glomerular-predominant amyloid as AL without formal typing
Assuming that a negative family history excludes a hereditary cause
Overlooking the option of combined liver and kidney transplantation
Missing the diagnosis in older sporadic presentations
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology, chapter on renal amyloidosis
Oxford Textbook of Medicine, chapter on hereditary amyloidosis
International Society of Amyloidosis nomenclature guidelines
management: Combined liver and kidney transplantation is potentially curative by removing the hepatic source of variant fibrinogen while replacing the failed kidney
For renal-limited disease, isolated kidney transplantation improves function but carries a risk of amyloid recurrence in the graft, which must be counselled
Supportive nephrological care of nephrotic syndrome with renin-angiotensin blockade for proteinuria and blood pressure, oedema management and treatment of dyslipidaemia
Renal replacement therapy by dialysis when end-stage kidney disease supervenes
Monitor proteinuria, renal function and blood pressure, using SAP scintigraphy to track organ amyloid burden
Genetic counselling and family screening for FGA variants given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance
